analysis.one_liner: Reclassifies broadband internet as a regulated telecommunications service, letting the FCC enforce net neutrality rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in July 2022 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written into law that broadband internet is a "telecommunications service" under the Communications Act. That matters because companies classified as telecommunications providers are common carriers, meaning the FCC can require them to treat all internet traffic equally and cannot charge websites for faster delivery. Internet providers are currently classified as "information services," which has allowed them to operate under lighter rules. The bill went to the Senate Commerce Committee and never advanced before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users would gain enforceable rules against internet providers blocking, slowing, or prioritizing online content for a fee, since common-carrier status would give the FCC clear power to regulate broadband directly. Households already pay some of the highest broadband prices among wealthy countries, and common-carrier status also opens the door to FCC scrutiny of rates and service quality. Website operators and small online businesses would benefit from not having to pay internet providers for faster access to their own customers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes broadband's classification as a telecommunications service directly into the Communications Act, so the FCC could forbid blocking, throttling, and paid fast lanes and enforce rules against discrimination in how internet traffic is handled.
Common-carrier status would also give the FCC broader authority to police rates, privacy, and the quality of broadband service generally.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers would bear the cost: reclassification would subject companies like the major cable and telecom carriers to common-carrier obligations, ending their ability to sell paid fast lanes and exposing them to FCC oversight of rates and practices.

drawbacks.text: Classifying broadband as a telecommunications service would impose common-carrier obligations on internet providers, which the industry argues could raise compliance costs and dampen investment in broadband networks.
The bill enacts the reclassification by statute rather than through the FCC's ordinary rulemaking process, removing the flexibility of case-by-case regulatory design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—restoring enforceable net neutrality and giving the FCC clear authority over broadband—was real, and the cost to internet users of its failure is continued uncertainty over blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization, which have so far been limited by state laws and court rulings rather than federal statute. The main cost of passage would have fallen on internet providers in the form of common-carrier regulation, and their objection—possible overreach slowing investment—was plausible but not demonstrated. The bill was never vetted in committee or on the floor, so its real-world tradeoffs were never openly weighed, and its death ended not by argument but by lack of a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee after introduction and never advanced to a vote or even a committee markup before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 28, 2022, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action followed: it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or consideration in the House before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers like the major cable and wireless carriers benefit, since they remain outside common-carrier regulation, and the FCC's ability to police blocking, throttling, and paid fast lanes stays unresolved.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to classify broadband as a telecommunications service.

for.name: 29 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 27 of 48 Senate Democrats and both Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senator Cantwell, chair of the Commerce Committee to which it was referred.

against.name: Broadband and cable industry
against.role: Internet service providers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Long campaigned against reclassifying broadband as a telecommunications service, arguing it would impose heavy common-carrier regulation; no provider action on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 29 cosponsors were Republicans; no Republican supported the bill in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where any cross-party support could have been tested.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable, telecom, and wireless carriers)
industries.note: Reclassifying broadband as a telecommunications service would subject these companies to common-carrier duties, allowing the FCC to restrict paid prioritization, blocking, and throttling and to scrutinize rates. The bill's death leaves them largely outside that regulatory regime.

industries.industry: Edge and content companies (streaming, search, social media, online retailers)
industries.note: Strong net neutrality rules protect these firms from internet providers charging them or their users for priority access; they gain from the bill and lose from its failure, though they were not direct parties to it.
